rv.q: What's important is that the thing is all smart and all enjoyable and all very good for the theater.
This autobiographical musical about a young black man's search for artistic authenticity is a rock concert, a coming-of-age story and a meditation on identity rolled into one electrifying package.
Passing Strange is a theatrical memoir that works because it tells a specific story with universal resonance, and because Stew has the rare ability to make his personal journey feel like our own.

Directed by Annie Dorsen (who also gets some creative credit), "Passing Strange" is a mix of a rock concert and theater piece with the singer-songwriter-narrator anchored in the center of the action. It owes great stylistic debt to the Chicago-driven performance-poetry movement with its heavy emphasis on confession.
Passing Strange is so fresh and so unique, in fact, it's possible its author isn't aware how revolutionary it is on the Broadway landscape.
Whatever you call it, there is no doubt this is beguiling theater, a new form that refuses to be pigeon holed.
Passing Strange is a soul-stirring musical memoir about a young black artist's journey of self-discovery that pulses with the authentic voice of someone who has lived to tell his tale.

cn.t: Critics embrace this inventive rock musical memoir as smart, soul-stirring theater that defies Broadway convention, praising Stew's authentic voice and the show's electrifying blend of concert, coming-of-age story, and identity meditation.
